senses: from there, next; in the next or second place
la:adv:deinde.html:
dĕindĕ, and abbrev. dein (cf. P., and
exin, proin—in both forms ei is monosyl. in the class. poets; as dissyl.,; ), adv.
de-inde
, thereafter, thereupon (for syn. cf.: dein, exinde, inde, deinceps, post, postea, porro).—
In place (rare), from there, from that place: via interest perangusta, deinde paulo latior patescit campus,.—
Transf. in (local) succession, thereafter, next (cf. dehinc, no. I. B.): auxiliares Galli Germanique in fronte, post quos pedites sagittarii, dein quatuor legiones, exin totidem aliae legiones, etc.,next,: juxta Hermanduros Narisci, ac deinde Marcomanni,: haec quidem duo binis pedibus incisim: dein membratim, etc.,; cf. : Baliares locat ante signa ... dein graviorem armis peditem,.—
In time.
Thereafter, afterwards, then (common in all periods and styles): hostes contra legiones suas instruunt. Deinde utrique imperatores in medium exeunt,: accepit conditionem, dein quaestum occipit,: complures ex iis occiderunt: deinde se in castra receperunt,: dein Tubero, Nescio (inquit) Africane,: incipe, Damoeta; tu deinde sequēre, Menalca. Alternis dicetis,; unguibus et pugnis, dein fustibus, atque ita porro Pugnabant armis,: in Aequis nihil deinde memorabile actum,.—
Freq. after primum, principio, prius, inde, postea, postremo, etc.: Caesar primum suo, deinde omnium ex conspectu remotis equis, etc.,; cf. fin.; ; et saep.: principio duplicavit illum pristinum patrum numerum, deinde, etc.,: plebs montem sacrum prius, deinde Aventinum occupavit,; cf. : hunc secutus est Cursor. deinde L. Maso aedilicius: inde multi Masones ...: deinde Carbones et Turdi insequuntur,: jubent venire agros Attalensium ...: deinde agros in Macedonia regios ...: deinde agrum optimum et fructuosissimum Corinthium ...: post autem agros in Hispania ... tum vero ipsam veterem Carthaginem vendunt,: quippe oppidana lascivia invicem incessente probra, deinde saxa, postremo ferrum sumpsere, et saep.; so, corresp. with in praesentia,.—
Connected with tum, tunc, postea, porro, postremo, etc.: primum ea quae sumus acturi cogitare debemus, deinde tum dicere ac facere, Müll.; so, deinde tum,: deinde tunc,: tum deinde,: tunc deinde,: servos Milonis sibi confessos esse de interficiendo Cn. Pompeio conjurasse; deinde postea se gladio percussum esse, etc.,; so, deinde postea,: : ; ; : postea deinde,; ext. 5; cf. also deinde eam postea supprimat,: post deinde,; : deinde post,; : deinde porro,; : mox deinde,: deinde postremo,; cf.: deinde ad extremum,; : deinde deinceps, (dub.); id, Leg. 3, 2, 4; .—
Strengthened by cum, postquam, posteaquam, ubi, etc.: dein (deinde) cum,: deinde cum,as soon as,; cf.: dein cum,: deinde (dein) postquam,; ; et saep.: deinde posteaquam,: deinde (dein) ubi,; ; . —
Of future time, hereafter, from this time forward (rare): tu velim cures ut sciam, quibus nos dare oporteat eas, quas ad te deinde litteras mittemus,; cf. ; experiamini quidquid deinde fors tulerit,. —
In an enumeration or succession of facts or arguments, afterwards, next in order, then: ut a prima congressione maris et feminae, deinde a progenie et cognatione ordiar, etc.,: te ad coenas itare desisse moleste fero ... Deinde etiam vereor ... ne, etc.,; et saep.—
Esp. freq. following primum (primus), followed by postremo al.: quod in homine multo est evidentius, primum ex ea caritate, quae, etc., deinde, etc.,; ; ; ; et passim; cf. deinde, several times repeated,; ; : primum with deinde eight times, and finally postremo,: deinde ... tum ... post, etc.,; et saep.: deinde ... deinde ... postremo ...,: excellente tum Crasso et Antonio, deinde (next in the order of excellence, not of time) Philippo, post Julio, : deinde ... tum ... postremo,: prima nobilitas Cilicio ... dein Lyciae Olympo, mox Centuripino, etc.,; so after optimus,; ; after laudatissimus,; cf. : femur promovetur saepissime in interiorem: deinde in exteriorem: raro admodum in priorem aut posteriorem,.—
So, in a climax, emphasizing the last of a series: suis artibus, fraude, deinde insidiis est prope circumventus,at length, in fine,; ; cf. Hand, Turs. II. p. 238 -249.

la:adj:deinceps.html:
dĕin-ceps (dissyl., ; but trisyl. . Cf. dehinc and deinde), adj. and adv.
capio. Prop., taking place next or after, v. Corss. Ausspr. 2, 591; cf.: particeps, princeps
.
Adj. (gen. deincipis or deincipitis), following thereafter, next following: deinceps qui deinde cepit, ut princeps qui primum cepit, Paul. ex Müll.; cf.: deincipem antiqui dicebant proxime quemque captum ut principem primum captum,. So only: deincipiti die, Ap. Flor. no. 16, p. 353, 33.—
Adv., in a constant series, one after another, successively, in turn, = ἑξῆς or ἐφεξῆς (for syn. cf.: deinde, exinde, inde, indidem, post, postea, porro—freq. and good prose).
In space: arboribus deinceps constitutis,: his (saxis) collocatis et coagmentatis alius insuper ordo adicitur, etc.... sic deinceps omne opus contexitur,; cf. : ea quae ἀκροστιχίς dicitur, cum deinceps ex primis versuum litteris aliquid conectitur, ; cf. : prima ... ac deinceps,.—
In time: duo deinceps reges civitatem auxerunt,: ut deinceps qui accubarent canerent ad tibiam clarorum virorum laudes,: trīs fratres, quos video deinceps tribunos plebis per triennium fore,; cf. : clamore significant, hunc alii deinceps excipiunt, etc.,.—Esp. freq. with alii, reliqui, multi, omnes, totus: stationes dispositas haberent atque alios alii deinceps exciperent,; cf. ; : receperunt Arverni eum deincepsque aliae gentes,; ; et saep.: reliquis deinceps diebus Caesar silvas caedere instituit,; cf. ; 7, 23; : possum deinceps totam rem explicare, deinde ad extremum, etc.,; .—
In order.
With ordinals (rare): septimus sum deinceps praetorius in gente nostra,the seventh in succession,; cf. .—
In denoting the successive parts of a discourse: de justitia satis dictum est: deinceps, ut erat propositum, de beneficentia ac de liberalitate dicatur, i. e. ordine sic ferente,successively, in order,; cf. ; 3, 2, 7.—
To indicate an immediate sequence: si non ab eo, in quo proxime desitum, deinceps incipietur,; cf. : annales Ennii ut deinceps legi possint,that they may be read on continuously,; . In this use deinceps is often very nearly = deinde, ; —
In particular combinations.
Deinde deinceps, inde deinceps, postea deinceps, Gr. ἔπειτα ἑξῆς: deinde etiam deinceps posteris prodebatur,; cf. ; ; : deinceps inde multae, quas non minus diligenter elaboratas ... afferebamus,; so, deinceps inde,: inde deinceps,: aequitate sua postea trium regum bellis deinceps omnibus functum officiis,. —
Corresp. with primus: primum est officium, ut se conservet in naturae statu: deinceps, ut ea teneat, quae, etc.,; cf.: principes sint patria et parentes ... proximi liberi totaque domus ... deinceps bene convenientes propinqui,, and .—
Hence, after enumerations, in phrases like Eng. and so forth: ut prima (officia) diis immortalibus, secunda patriae, tertia parentibus, deinceps gradatim reliqua reliquis debeantur,and so on; cf.: nam et in prooemio primum est aliquid et secundum ac deinceps,; ; cf. : et deinceps, ac deinceps,and so forth,—
Perge deinceps, go on, : gallinae villaticae sunt, quas deinceps rure habent in villis,continually,; cf. Hand, Turs. II. p. 232-238.

la:verb:deicio.gloss: to throw, cast, or hurl down; precipitate
senses: to throw, cast, or hurl down; precipitate
la:verb:deicio.html:
dē-ĭcĭo or dejicio, jēci, jectum, 3, v. a.
jacio
,
to throw or cast down; to hurl down, precipitate (very freq., and class.).
Lit.
In gen.: araneas de foribus et de pariete,: aliquem de ponte in Tiberim,; cf.: aliquem e ponte,: aliquem de saxo (Tarpeio),; ; ; cf. aliquem saxo Tarpeio,: aliquem equo,; : jugum servile a cervicibus,: togam ab umeris,; cf.: togam de umero,; esp. reflex. with pron.: se de muro,; cf.: se de superiore parte aedium,: se per munitiones,: se a praealtis montibus (venti),: librum in mare,; cf.: aliquem in locum inferiorem,: aliquem e summo in Tartara,: elatam securim in caput (regis),; cf. : equum e campo in cavam hanc viam,force to leap down,: bustum aut monumentum, aut columnam,; so, statuas veterum hominum (c. c. depellere simulacra deorum),: monumenta regis templaque Vestae,: signa aenea in Capitolio (tempestas),: omnes Hermas,: turrim,; cf. arces, et saep.: arbores,to fell,; : caput uno ictu,to cut off,; : libellos,to tear down,; (but , antemnis disjectis is the true reading): comam, Afran. ap. ; cf.: crinibus dejectis,loose, dishevelled,: sortes,to cast into the urn,: dejectam aerea sortem accepit galea,: cum dejecta sors esset,; cf.: pernam, glandium,to throw into the pot,: alvum,to purge,; cf.: casei caprini, qui facillimi deiciantur,i. e. are most easily digested,; opp. alvum superiorem,i. e. to vomit,.—
Esp.
Milit. t. t., to drive out, dislodge an enemy from his position: hostes muro turribusque dejecti, Caes. B. G. 7, 28; cf.: nostri dejecti sunt loco,: praesidium ex saltu,; cf.: agmen Gallorum ex rupe Tarpeia,: ex tot castellis,: praesidium Claternā,; cf.: praesidium loco summe munito,: praesidium (without abl.), ; ; : castra hostium,to destroy,: praetorium, et saep.—
Jurid. t. t., to drive out, turn out of possession, eject, dispossess (cf. deduco): unde vi prohibitus sis ... unde dejectus?; cf. : nisi ex eo loco ubi vestigium impresserit, deici neminem posse,fin.: aliquem de possessione imperii,.—
Naut. t. t., pass.: deici, to be driven out of one's course: naves ad inferiorem partem insulae,: classis tempestate vexata ad Balearīs insulas deicitur,; .—
Pregn. (cf.: cado, concĭdo, decĭdo; caedo, concīdo, decīdo, etc.), to fell with a mortal wound, to bring down dead to the ground; to kill, slay: his dejectis et coacervatis cadaveribus,; ; ; ; cf.: quem telo primum, quem postremum aspera virgo Deicis?: avem ab alto caelo,; cf. : Glaucoque bovem Thetidique juvencam Deicit Ancaeus,i. e. slaughters as a sacrifice,: super juvencum stabat dejectum leo,: (Hercules) aves sagittis dejecit,: gruem,.—
To lower, let down, hang down, depress, of the head, etc. (cf. II. A. infra): dejecto capite (opp. supino capite),.—Of a nod (opp. relato capite), Apul. Met. 10.—Of a wild beast: id (caput) dejectum semper in terram,: in pectora mentum,: euntes dejecta cervice Getae,.—
Trop.
In gen.: pueri Sisennae oculos de isto numquam deicere,never took their eyes off him,; cf. : oculos a republica,: dejecit vultum et demissa voce locuta est,cast down her eyes,; cf.: oculos in terram,; and in Gr. construction, dejectus oculos,with downcast eyes,: dejectus vultum,: ecquid ergo intellegis quantum mali de humana condicione dejeceris?thou hast removed, averted,; cf.: quantum de doloris terrore,: vitia a se ratione,; cf.: cruciatum a corpore (with depellere omnia verbera),: hunc metum Siciliae,fin.: quae replenda vel deicienda sunt,: eum de sententia dejecistis,hast diverted from his opinion,: fortis et constantis est, non tumultuantem de gradu deici, ut dicitur,; cf. .—
In partic. (acc. to no. I. B. 2.), to cast one down from the prospect of a thing; to prevent from obtaining, to deprive, rob of: de honore deici,: de possessione imperii,; for which, ad deiciendum honore eum,; and, dejecti honore,; so with simple abl.: aliquem aedilitate,: aedilitate,: praeturā,: principatu,: certo consulatu,: spe,: ea spe,; cf.: opinione trium legionum (i. e. spe trium legionum colligendarum),: conjuge tanto,. —Without abl.: M. Caelium mentio illa fatua ... subito dejecit, etc., Cael. ap. : cum inimicum eo quoque anno petentem dejecisset,: uxorem (sc. conjugio),: hoc dejecto,after his fall,; cf. ; : ex alto dejectus culmine regni,.—
To humble: deicimur, sed non perimus,: deiciendi hominis causa,.—Hence, dejectus, a, um, P. a. (very rare).
Sunk down, low: equitatus noster etsi dejectis atque inferioribus locis constiterat,: dejectius,—
(Acc. to no. II. B., deprived of hope; hence) Cast down, dejected, dispirited: haud dejectus equum duci jubet,; cf.:

haud sic dejecta, : in epilogis plerumque dejecti et infracti sumus, —Sup. does not occur.— * Adv.dējectē, low; only comp., dejectius,

la:noun:deiectus.html:
dējectus, ūs, m.
deicio
,
a casting or throwing down (rare; not in Cic.).
In gen.: arborum,: gravis (Penei),fall,; cf. fluminum,: aquae,; and absol., ; cf. .—
Concr., that which is thrown over, a covering: velatum geminae dejectu lyncis,.—
Esp., of localities (acc. to dejectus, P. a., I.), a declivity, descent: collis,: in dejectu positus,. In plur.: collis ex utraque parte lateris dejectūs habebat,.—
Transf., the lowering of the voice, = Gr. θέσις (opp. elatio, = Gr. ἄρσις), .

la:noun:deiectio.html:
dējectĭo, ōnis, f.
deicio
,
a throwing or casting down or out (rare).
Lit. (acc. to deicio no. 1 A. and B.): imaginum,.—
Esp.

Medic. t. t.: alvi,a purging,; : dejectio alone,.—

Esp., legal t. t., ejection, a turning out of possession: qui illam vim dejectionemque fecerit, * ; .—
(Acc. to dejectus, P. a. no. I.) Altitudines stellarum et dejectiones, depressions, Firmic. Math. 2, 3.—
Trop.: gradūs dejectio,degradation,: populi nostri, Mac. 3, 43.—(, defectione is prob. the true reading.)

la:other:Deianira.html:
Dēïănīra, ae, f., Δηϊάνειρα,
daughter of Oeneus, sister of Meleager, wife of Hercules, and mother of Hyllus. She involuntarily caused the death of Hercules, by sending him the garment Nessus had given her, ; ; ; ; ; .
